activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it really is, so people who disagree with us must be uninformed or biased.
story:
The group chat had been peaceful for exactly one afternoon, which Chloe knew was a record. Then Emy posted a photo from the science fair, and Emeric replied, "wow, guess the judges only care about shiny posters," and within ten minutes the chat had blown up. Emy insisted the judges were fair. Emeric insisted they were biased against his project on mold growth. Chloe watched the messages dwindle from paragraphs to single angry words, then read the whole fight again from the top, hunting for the hidden thing that had set it off.

She typed, "Wait. Emeric, which project won?" Emeric said the one with the remote-controlled glacier. Emy said, "That's not why it won, it won because the data was good." Chloe frowned at her screen. They had both been standing in the same humid gym for the same two hours, watching the same three judges, and they had come out with two different fairs, as if the gym itself had split in half. That felt like a puzzle with a rule behind it, something you couldn't see directly but could test. So she tried an experiment: she sent each of them the same question in a private message, "What do you think the other person would say happened?"

Emy wrote back, "Emeric will say the judges were unfair because he doesn't know how scoring works." Emeric wrote back, "Emy will say the judges were fine because she always takes the teacher's side." Chloe stared at the two answers. Each of them believed they saw the science fair exactly as it really was, plain as a photo, and each one decided the other had to be either uninformed or biased. Neither one wondered if they might both be looking through their own particular eyeballs. She screenshotted nothing, because that felt like tattling, but she did copy both sentences into her notes app with the heading EVIDENCE.

The next morning she asked Ms. Mehta in the hallway, "Is there a word for when two people think they see reality and assume the other one is dumb or biased?" Ms. Mehta said, "That's called naive realism," and kept walking, which was somehow perfect. At lunch Chloe posted in the chat: "You're both sure you saw the real fair. Emy, you think Emeric lacks info. Emeric, you think Emy's biased. You're doing the exact same thing to each other." Then she added, "Also, mold project was gross but brave." There was a long pause, three dots appearing and vanishing, until Emeric wrote, "fine, the glacier was cool," and Emy wrote, "fine, the mold data was actually decent." Chloe put her phone face down and poked her straw through her juice pouch, victorious, like the end of a dynasty of arguments.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Julius Caesar reported a quick victory at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC with three Latin words, 'Veni, vidi, vici': I came, I saw, I conquered.
story:
Mason stood in the kitchen holding seven index cards, each one jammed with facts about volcanoes. Ms. Gupta had said every speech needed an opening hook, three points and a closing, and his was due tomorrow. Three points felt impossible. How could he pick only three from seven?

"Drayden says three is all anyone remembers," said his little sister, chewing a granola bar at the counter. She wanted to watch her show, and he was blocking the screen. Mason moved aside, but his eyes caught the history book she had left open on the table, the one with Rome on the cover.

There it was. Julius Caesar reported a quick victory at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC with three Latin words, "Veni, vidi, vici." Mason read it twice. I came, I saw, I conquered. Two thousand years later, even Mason, who could barely remember what he had eaten for breakfast, knew those words. Caesar could have written a whole report, Mason thought, but he didn't. Maybe that was the trick, three short punches instead of one long muddy river.

He tested it right there in the kitchen. He read his sister all seven cards about volcanoes. She stared at him, dull-eyed, and said "hot rocks" when he asked what she remembered. Then he picked three cards, the most influential ones, and stacked the rest under them like a hierarchy of importance, best on top, weakest at the bottom. He read only the top three. When he finished, she actually looked up. "Wait, the ash can poison the sky? That's the good part."

"See? You generate more interest with less," Mason said, surprising himself. She shrugged and reached for the remote, but he was already crossing out cards, narrowing his volcano down to how they form, what they destroy, and the ash that chokes the whole sky. Three points, like three Latin words marching in a row.

He set the surviving cards on the counter and raised his pencil like a sword. "Veni, vidi, vici," he announced to the kitchen. His sister threw a pillow at him.

activity: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
knowledge_domain: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
fact: The Roman Empire was permanently divided in 395 CE, when Emperor Theodosius I died and his two sons each took one half, east and west.
story:
Hazel spread the giant map of the Roman Empire across her grandfather's kitchen table, weighting the corners with a jar of pickles and two coasters. She had a history quiz on Monday, and somehow drawing the borders was supposed to help her digest the whole mess of why Rome fell apart. The map smelled like old paper and faintly like the pickles, and the Mediterranean glowed a luminous blue in the afternoon sun.

Then her little brother thundered in, grabbed the eastern edge, and hollered that he wanted the half with the fancy cities. Hazel yanked it back. "You can't just split something down the middle because you want to!"

Their grandfather shuffled over with his tea and looked at the two of them tugging at the paper, and he laughed so hard he nearly spilled the cup. "You know," he said, "an emperor named Theodosius the First did exactly that. When he died in the year 395, his two sons each took one half of the whole empire, east and west. Permanent. No take-backs."

Hazel froze with her hand still on the map. Wait. Wait wait wait. Two brothers. Two halves. She flashed back to the school hallway where Michaela had groaned, "There are too many dates, how does anyone remember the year it divided?" and Agathe had shrugged and said she would just guess 400-something. Hazel had guessed wrong too, on the practice quiz. But now the number was stuck to a story, a story about arguing brothers, and she would never lose it.

"Grandpa, that's it. That's the whole quiz question," she said, and she grabbed a marker. On the eastern half she wrote BIG BROTHER and on the western half she wrote LITTLE BROTHER, exactly where her own brother's fists were planted. She laughed, then copied the date, 395, along the dividing line in huge numbers. "Monday, you are going down."

Her brother, still gripping his half of the map, said, "I want the east. It has more pickles."

"It's a map," Hazel said. "There are no pickles."

"Then I want the coasters."

activity: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
knowledge_domain: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
fact: Python's print() starts a new line after each output by default; adding end=' ' keeps the next output on the same line.
story:
Luke had ten minutes left before Mr. Ma collected everyone's screens, and his times table program still printed like a staircase gone wrong. He had drafted the loop on paper first, the way Mr. Ma suggested, and the math was right: seven times one is seven, seven times two is fourteen, all the way to seven times twelve. The problem was that every answer landed on its own line, marching down the screen like ants, and Mr. Ma wanted the whole table to fit in one tidy row before the coding club bell.

Kristina leaned over from the next keyboard. "Mine does the staircase thing too. I assumed the numbers would just flow together."

"Mine assumed that too," Luke said. "The computer had other plans." The lab smelled like dry-erase marker and someone's grape gum, and the clock above the door ticked louder than a clock should.

Luke tried putting all twelve answers into one print, with commas, but that gave him a row of brackets he hadn't asked for. Then he noticed something in the sheet Mr. Ma had left on the front desk. He squinted at it. print() starts a new line after each output by default, the sheet said, but adding end=' ' keeps the next output on the same line. That was it. Not the numbers, not the loop. The print itself was cutting the line every time.

"Try end equals space," Luke whispered to Kristina. He typed it into his loop, right inside the parentheses, and ran the program. The twelve answers slid across the screen in one row: 7 14 21 28, all the way to 84, like beads on a string.

"Show me," Kristina said, and copied the fix just as Pearl wandered by eating a pretzel.

"You two look like you invented fire," Pearl said.

"We invented one row," Luke said. "Out of twelve lines. Don't be gullible, it happens all the time in this club."

Mr. Ma stopped behind them and read the screen. "One row," he said. "Nice. Two minutes left, everyone."

Luke ran it again with a nine instead of a seven, and the new table unrolled across the screen in one clean line, all the way to 108.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: According to the U.S. CDC, adults catch an average of two to three colds a year, and children often catch more.
story:
Vincent was stuck at his grandmother's house for the third day in a row, his nose red as a stop sign and his pile of used tissues growing like a small snowdrift beside the couch. This was his third cold since fall, and it made him furious. Nobody else in his family seemed to catch anything, ever. His grandmother brought him toast and honey, and the radiator continued to radiate a steady heat that made him sleepy, but he was too annoyed to nap.

"I don't get it," he said when she collected his plate. "I got my third cold since fall and you got zero. That's not fair."

She laughed from the doorway. "Grown-ups only average two to three colds a whole year. Kids your age often catch more than that." Then she went off to the kitchen, humming, as if she hadn't just handed him a mystery.

Vincent sat up straight, tissues tumbling off his lap. If it was normal for kids, then other kids should be getting colds too, not just him. He grabbed his phone and texted Pedro: "How many colds have you had since fall?" Then Marylou. Then, because his grandmother had moved on to her leisure time in the garden, he hobbled to the window and watched her pull carrots out of the frozen ground while he waited.

Pedro answered first. "Two. Plus a sinus thing, so basically three." Marylou's reply came five minutes later. "Four, but my mom says I count everything." Four! Even Ms. Krause, his teacher, had only missed one day all winter, and she'd said it was a dentist appointment.

Vinanto made a chart on the back of a grocery receipt, one column for kids and one for grown-ups, and the kids' side filled up fast. He stared at it, feeling something loosen in his chest, which was definitely just relief and not another symptom.

"Grandma!" he shouted toward the garden. "Your generation is radical at not getting sick, but I have data now!"

She poked her head in the door, carrots in her hand. "Show me," she said. "Bring the chart to the table, and I'll put the kettle on."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi as the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur.
story:
Brooke followed her mother through the doors of the community hall, where the smell of fried food hung in the air and a speaker crackled somewhere near the stage. The whole building buzzed with people in bright orange and blue, and a line of kids already stretched past the dessert table. Brooke's cousin Avneet waved from beside a folding table stacked with paper flags.

"You're just in time," Avneet said. "The nagar kirtan, the procession, leaves in twenty minutes."

Brooke had come for the food, honestly, and for the part where everyone danced in the parking lot. But as they waited, a small boy tugged on the sleeve of a man carrying a drum and asked, "Why is today important? Everyone keeps saying Vaisakhi."

The man crouched down. "Because in 1699, at Anandpur, the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa," he said. He stood, adjusted his drum strap, and was swallowed by the crowd.

Brooke turned the sentence over while she helped Avneet carry a tray of paper cups. Khalsa. She'd heard the word at school when a classmate named Sarah had given a presentation, but Brooke had only half listened. She tried to summarize it for herself and got stuck. What was the Khalsa, a place, a book, a group? The man had said it was founded, like a club or a city.

She tested it. If it was founded by a Guru, maybe it was the community itself, the people. She walked up to three different people and asked each one the same thing: "Are you Khalsa?"

The first man pointed at his orange turban and said, "Yes." The second woman laughed and said, "My brother is, I'm still deciding." The third, a teenage boy carrying a flag, said, "That's why we march today."

Three people, three answers that fit a group and not a place. Brooke found Avneet at the front of the procession as the drums started, and the crowd felt buoyant, everyone moving together like a single wave rolling toward the doors. A laser pointer of afternoon sun cut through the high window and landed on the flag pole.

"That's it," Brooke said, pointing at the flag. "People, not a place."

Avneet handed her a flag. "You carry it, then."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Museums control temperature and humidity because changes make wood, paper and canvas swell and shrink, which can crack or warp old objects.
story:
Christopher had exactly forty minutes to find out why a tiny metal dial sat inside a glass case next to a two-hundred-year-old wooden mask. The field trip buses left at two o'clock, and Mr. Yilmaz had already warned the class twice about wandering off.

"Come look at this," Christopher called to Jaelyn, who was busy sketching the mask for the art assignment due tomorrow. She wanted the best sketch in class, and she was not going to waste her last half hour on a thermometer.

"It's a thermometer," she said without looking up.

"It's not," Christopher said. "There are two needles. One says sixty-eight, but the other says fifty and has a little H next to it. That's humidity. But why would the museum measure that?"

He leaned closer to the case. The mask had a thin crack running down one cheek, and a small card beside it read "fragile." Christopher thought about the wooden fence behind his house, which shrank in dry August weather until the gaps widened, then swelled again in the rain of September. If air could do that to a fence in one season, what could it do to a mask over two centuries?

He found Mr. Yilmaz near the mummy exhibit and asked about the dial. Before the teacher could answer, Kristina, who was eavesdropping as usual, said, "The guide told our group earlier. Museums control temperature and humidity because changes make wood, paper and canvas swell and shrink, which can crack or warp old objects."

"So the dial is checking whether the case is staying the same," Christopher said. He revised his whole picture of the museum. It was not just a building full of old things; it was a machine for keeping them still, protecting the heritage in every case.

At ten minutes to two, he raced back to Jaelyn. "Your mask. Draw the crack. If the humidity in there ever jumps, that crack gets worse."

Jaelyn looked at her sketch, then at the mask, and added the crack with one careful line.

"Bus!" Mr. Yilmaz shouted from the doorway.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages, so something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found.
story:
The bus smelled like wet jackets and oranges. Mathis sat three rows from the back with his knees against the seat in front of him, phone flat on his thigh. Emerson leaned over from the aisle seat.

"Everyone screenshotted it before you deleted it," Emerson said. "Even people from Jeanne's brother's grade."

"I know," Mathis said. He had typed the post at eleven at night, in ALL CAPS, with about forty exclamation points, claiming the seventh-grade bake sale money had been stolen and naming a name. By morning he had deleted it, but the comments had already spread through half the school network. He had learned one thing fast: typing in all caps read as shouting even when you didn't mean to shout.

Jeanne slid into the seat across the aisle. "It's gone, though," she said. "You took it down before first bell."

"Gone from my page," Mathis said. "Not gone gone." He had been thinking about that all through science. A post was like shouting on the bus: private meant whispering to one person, public meant standing up and yelling, and the whole internet was the second kind. Once you yelled, you couldn't un-yell it into everyone's ears.

"So it's deleted," Jeanne said.

"Mr. Holloway told my sister something last year," Emerson said. "She deleted a page for her club, and he said the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages, so something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found."

Mathis looked at his phone. The bus jolted over the tracks near Mr. Holloway's street, and his grip felt frail for a second before he tightened it. He typed the Wayback Machine's address, then his old post's web address from memory, because he had checked it so many times the night he wrote it.

"Here's the test," he said out loud, mostly to himself. "If it saved my page, I can retrieve the exact words and at least see what everyone's screenshot came from." He tapped the button that searched for old copies.

A calendar appeared. A snapshot existed from two days ago, taken at 7:04 in the morning, twelve minutes after he had posted and forty before he deleted it. He opened it. There was the post, all caps, all forty exclamation points, the name in it.

Jeanne leaned across the aisle and read it. "You have to talk to Dario," she said. "That's the real problem. The post isn't."

"He rides the next bus," Mathis said. He saved the link, put the phone in his pocket, and pulled the yellow cord two stops early so he could walk to Dario's street.

"Tell him the shout was mine," he said to Emerson, and stepped down into the rain.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: A pill organizer has a compartment for each day of the week, so an empty compartment shows that day's dose has already been taken.
story:
Alice stood at the arrivals gate watching the sliding doors open and close, holding a sign that said GRANDPA in blue marker. Around her, travelers in winter coats pulled suitcases toward families who waved and shouted, and somewhere a speaker crackled announcements about a delayed flight from Toronto. Her grandpa had never visited alone before, and Mom had warned her twice on the drive over that the whole week would depend on Alice paying attention, because Grandpa forgot things now.

He came through the doors in a gray cardigan, smaller than she remembered, carrying one old leather bag. "There's my scientist," he said, and Alice ran to hug him.

The first two days went well. Grandpa told stories about the migratory birds that used to pass over his old farmhouse every October, and he helped her plant marigold seeds in cups on the windowsill. "They'll germinate in about a week," he said, patting the soil. "Right about when I fly home."

On the third morning, Alice found him standing in the kitchen holding a small blue box, turning it over in his hands. "Did I take my morning pills or didn't I?" he muttered. "I can't recall, and I can't take them twice."

Alice's heart sank. Mom was already at work, and Grandpa's face had gone pale with worry. She looked at the blue box in his hand and noticed it had seven little compartments along the top, each one labeled with a letter. She counted them under her breath: S, M, T, W, T, F, S. One for every day of the week.

"Grandpa, what day is it?" she asked.

"Wednesday, I think. Yes, Wednesday."

Alice slid her fingernail under the lid marked W and opened it. Empty. She opened the Tuesday one too, also empty, and then Thursday's, which was full of little white and yellow pills. "Then you took them," she said. "Today's compartment is empty, and tomorrow's is still full, so the morning dose is gone."

Grandpa laughed, a big relieved laugh that made him seem taller. "A pill organizer with a door for each day of the week. You just solved it like a detective." He set the box on the counter where she could see it, and patted her shoulder. "From now on, we check the box, not my memory."

Alice called Kiara that afternoon to tell her about it, and Kiara suggested they make a chart of Grandpa's whole week so Alice could fill in what he did each day. Alice taped it to the refrigerator next to the marigold cups, where a tiny green sprout was just pushing up through the soil.

On Saturday, Grandpa stood in front of the chart, squinting at it, and Alice came up beside him. She opened the Saturday compartment of the blue box and held it out to him. "Empty," she said. "Now we wait for Sunday."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Airplane mode turns off a phone's radio signals, including the cellular connection it uses for calls and texts.
story:
At the start of science, Ms. Chowdhury collected the permission slips for Friday's field trip and said anyone who hadn't turned one in by the end of the day could not go. Sophie raised her hand. "My mom signed it this morning. She took a photo of it with my phone and said she'd email it to you." Her new phone, three days old, sat in her backpack. It was the first one she'd ever owned, and she'd promised to keep it off and zipped away during class.

At lunch she checked it. Ms. Chowdhury had emailed back that nothing had arrived. Sophie frowned. The little bars at the top of the screen were missing, and the words "airplane mode" glowed in the corner. She slid down the hall to find Boston, who was setting up the board game he'd brought.

"You have to help me," she said. "Mom sent the slip, but Ms. Chowdhury never got it. If it doesn't come through before last period, I miss the trip." Boston looked at the screen. "Airplane mode," he read. "My cousin's phone did that once. It turns off the radio signals, even the cellular connection, so calls and texts can't get through either. My aunt missed a whole day of messages."

Sophie thought about that. If the radio signals were off, then the phone wasn't talking to anything at all. It could sit there all afternoon and nothing would arrive. There was only one way to test it. She tapped the icon, and the bars reappeared. Immediately, a chime: the email from her mom, with the photo of the signed slip attached. "Yes!" Sophie hurried to the classroom, where Ms. Chowdhury was watering the plants that saturated the windowsill in green.

"Found it," Sophie said, holding out the phone. "It was in airplane mode. All fixed."

Ms. Chowdhury peered at the screen. "Good. You can keep it on your desk until the end of the day, then off it goes."

"Deal," Sophie said, and slid it to the corner of the desk, face up and quiet.

"Is that the equivalent of putting it away?" Boston asked from the doorway, grinning.

"Close enough," said Ms. Chowdhury, and marked Sophie's name off her list.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, and the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10.
story:
Grandpa's living room smelled like chili and popcorn, and every chair was taken. Luke sat on the floor between Ireland and Ruben, watching the pregame show while the screen flashed old black-and-white footage of helmet-carrying players.

"I remember the very first one," Grandpa announced from his recliner. "The Green Bay Packers against the Kansas City Chiefs. I was there in spirit, glued to the TV."

Luke turned around. "Wait. When was that exactly?"

"January 15, 1967," Grandpa said. "Cold as anything. Final score was 35 to 10, Packers."

Ruben leaned toward Luke and whispered, "Nobody can remember a score from that long ago. He's making it up."

Luke felt a flicker of resentment on Grandpa's behalf, but he also wanted to know if it was true. "I'm going to simulate the whole thing," he told Ireland. "We ask him questions we can check. If he really watched it, he'll get the easy stuff right, not just the score."

Ireland frowned. "And if he gets it wrong?"

"Then he guessed the numbers somehow, or someone told him."

Luke borrowed Grandpa's phone and typed while the national anthem played on TV. The first result matched everything: January 15, 1967, Packers over the Chiefs, 35 to 10. He scrolled twice more to be sure. Ruben looked over his shoulder and read it out loud, then slumped back against the couch. "Fine. He wasn't making it up."

"You sound pessimistic," Ireland said.

"I wanted him to be wrong. It would've been a better story."

Grandpa, who had been listening the whole time, stood up, walked over, and held out his hand. Luke gave back the phone. "You know how I remember the score?" Grandpa said. "My brother bet me a nickel on that game, and I've never let him forget it."

From the kitchen, Luke's dad called out that the chili was ready, and Grandpa headed straight for the door.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: A swimmer caught in a rip current can usually escape by swimming parallel to the beach, out of the narrow current, rather than straight against it.
story:
Emma had been at her aunt and uncle's beach house for two days, and she still couldn't categorize the ocean. Some minutes it seemed friendly, pushing foam around her ankles, and other minutes it looked like it was planning something. On the third morning, she and her cousin's friend Seraphina walked down to the sand while the adults unpacked the cooler, and Emma stopped in front of a yellow sign near the lifeguard stand.

"If the water pulls you out, swim sideways," Seraphina read aloud, squinting at the letters. "Sideways? That's weird. Wouldn't you swim straight back in?"

Emma studied the sign. It said rip currents were narrow, and that you should swim parallel to the beach instead of fighting straight against the pull. She filed that away the way she filed things before a test, not sure she'd need it. Then she and Seraphina ran into the waves, jumping the small ones, shrieking at the cold ones, until Emma noticed the sand beneath her feet had gone strange. The water was tugging her, steady and quiet, toward the deep.

She didn't panic, exactly, but her heart hammered. She tried swimming straight in, and the beach didn't get closer; the pulling got stronger, like the whole ocean had a spine made of muscle underneath her. She remembered the sign. Parallel to the beach. She turned sideways and swam, and after a stretch that felt long but probably wasn't, the pull vanished. She was out of the narrow strip of current, in ordinary water, and she swam straight in without any trouble at all.

Seraphina was waiting at the towel with a granola bar, her voice brittle with worry. "You went so far out. Are you okay?"

"It pulled me," Emma said, wringing out her hair. "But I went sideways, like the sign said, and it let go." She took the granola bar and split it in half, handing the bigger piece to Seraphina, and they sat watching the waves break sideways along the shore, one after another after another.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note's pitch depends on how fast the sound source vibrates: faster vibration makes a higher pitch, and slower vibration makes a lower one.
story:
Ruby sat on an overturned milk crate in her dad's garage, holding the guitar Zainab had lent her for the summer. The old paint cans in the corner smelled toxic, so Ruby had propped the side door open, and a warm breeze drifted in over the concrete floor. She had one week before Zainab came back from her trip, and she wanted to play a real song, not just strums.

The problem was the strings. Every time she thought she had them right, one of them sounded wrong, sour and low where it should have been bright. Kyler, who had biked over to watch, leaned against the workbench and plucked the thinnest string. "That one sounds kinda dead," he said. "Those nylon ones are a polymer, my cousin says, they stretch when they're new. Like they're still settling."

Ruby turned the tuning peg a little and plucked again. The note climbed, sharp and high, so she turned it back, and the note slid down like a bird dropping out of the air. She did it once more, slower, listening. Loosen the peg, the note dropped. Tighten it, the note rose. She frowned, thinking of the old wind chimes at her grandmother's house, how the thick tubes sounded low and the thin ones sang high. Maybe it wasn't only the string, maybe it was how fast it was moving, trembling quick for high and slow for low. She couldn't see the trembling, but she could hear it.

"I loosened this peg," she said, plucking the note and letting it fall, "and it went lower. Faster shaking means higher, slower means lower. I'm pretty sure that's the rule." Kyler nodded slowly, like he was filing it away.

They spent the next hour tuning all six strings, Ruby turning each peg a whisper at a time, Kyler calling out "higher" or "lower" from across the garage. When the sixth string finally rang true, the sound propelled through the open door and out into the street, where a dog started barking.

"Play the song," Kyler said. "Before it goes sour again."

Ruby set her fingers on the strings and began.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: Counting up is a quick way to check change: start at the price and add each coin and note handed back until you reach the amount you paid.
story:
The note in Tristan's pocket was short, because his mom had written it while loading the dryer: "Milk at Rosa's. Two dollars is small, four dollars is whole. Keep the receipt." Tristan read it twice, then once more under the flickering light of the laundromat. The machines drummed around him like a marching band, and his whole body felt buzzy, because this was the first time he would walk to the corner store alone. Ryan had done it months ago and never stopped bragging. Now it was Tristan's turn.

He marched the two blocks with his fist closed around a five dollar note, repeating the words so he would not modify his mission: milk, small, two dollars. Rosa's bell clattered when he pushed the door. He found the small milk, set it on the counter, and handed over his five. The cashier gave him back a handful: a note, coins, a receipt. Outside, on the curb, Tristan stared at it and his stomach dropped. Was this right? He had no idea how to check.

Then Zakariya biked past, skidded to a stop, and peered over his shoulder. "You look like you saw a ghost." "I got change and I can't tell if it's right," Tristan admitted. Zakariya grinned. "Count up. Start at the price and add each coin and note handed back until you reach the amount you paid." Tristan tried it out loud, milk on his knee. "Two dollars, plus a dollar makes three, plus a fifty makes three fifty, plus another fifty makes four, plus a dollar makes five." He looked up, wide-eyed. "It lands exactly on five. It's right!"

He ran the whole way back, milk swinging, and burst through the laundromat door. "Mom! I counted up and the change was perfect!" She laughed and held out her hand, and he dropped the coins into her palm, still warm from his grip, one by one.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Blue-enriched light from phone screens can reduce or delay the body's release of melatonin, the hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening.
story:
On Saturday morning, Dad handed Owen a small box, and Owen actually cheered. His first phone. He spent the whole day setting it up, and by evening he had downloaded a game, three chat apps, and a video app that Finnegan swore was the best one ever made. At nine thirty, Dad said, "Phone charges in the kitchen tonight," but Owen begged until Dad agreed to let him keep it in his room, just this once.

Owen lay in bed scrolling. The videos were hilarious, and he kept thinking, just one more, until eleven. When he finally closed his eyes, sleep would not come. He tossed. He turned. He stared at the ceiling until after midnight. The next morning he was so tired he put milk in the cereal box.

The following night the same thing happened, and the night after that too. By Wednesday, Owen was yawning through Ms. Li's class and Rowan whispered, "You look like a zombie." That afternoon, Owen sat at the kitchen table and thought it through like a mystery. The problem had started the exact night he got the phone. He wasn't worried about anything. His room was the same. The only thing that had changed was the screen.

He messaged Finnegan: "Do you scroll in bed?" Finnegan wrote back, "Every night, why?" Then, a minute later: "Wait. I never fall asleep fast either. My sister says screen light holds back your melatonin. It's the hormone that makes you sleepy at night." Owen read the message twice. That was it. That was the hidden cause.

He decided to test it. For three nights, he left the phone charging in the kitchen and read a paper book instead. On the third night he was asleep in fifteen minutes. On Saturday he marched to Dad with his results, holding a chart he had drawn with checkmarks.

"There was a delay in my melatonin," Owen announced. "The screen light did it. So the phone sleeps in the kitchen. That's the rule."

Dad grinned. "A rule from the scientist himself. Deal."

Owen shook his hand on it.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: On the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, published in 1967, both changing residence and changing schools are listed as life events that require readjustment.
story:
The office smelled like pencil shavings and lemon cleaner, and Kaitlyn sat with her hands pressed under her thighs so nobody would see them shaking. This was her third day at the new school, and her stomach had hurt since the first. Not the throwing-up kind, more like a stone she'd swallowed. Her mother had sent her to see Ms. Byrne, the counselor, because of the note Kaitlyn's teacher had passed along: Kaitlyn hadn't touched her lunch, not once. Ms. Byrne was talking to someone in the hallway, so Kaitlyn sat alone, staring at the papers scattered across the desk.

A single sheet had slid halfway off the stack, close enough to read upside down. She'd gotten good at reading upside down at her old school, where she and Lenny used to trade answers to crossword puzzles across the desk. Her eyes moved over the heading: the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, published in 1967. Below it was a long list of life events that require readjustment. She scanned down the column. There it was, plain as anything. Changing residence. And further down, changing schools. Both on the same list.

"So that's it," she whispered. It wasn't germs. It wasn't her stomach turning rebellious for no reason, though she'd started to wonder if her whole body was staging some kind of protest. Two things on that list had happened to her in the same month: the move out of the old apartment, and this school. No wonder she felt like a puzzle someone had shaken in the box. She decided to test it. If the list was right, then the feeling should be worse on days when things changed more, and better on days when nothing new happened. Wednesday, when she'd gotten lost looking for the gym and ended up in the boiler room, had been the worst day yet. That fit. Tuesday, when she'd found the library and stayed there all lunch, had been almost okay. That fit too.

She was still bent over the paper when the door opened. She jerked upright, feeling like she'd been caught doing something wrong, though it had just been lying there.

"That's not a secret, you know," Ms. Byrne said. She sat down and turned the sheet right side up, sliding it toward Kaitlyn. "Anyone can look."

"Then it's true?" Kaitlyn asked. "Moving and switching schools, both of them, they really count as things that need readjusting? In 1967 someone actually wrote that down?"

"Published in 1967, that's the one," Ms. Byrne said. "You're allowed to feel wobbly. It's practically the rules."

Kaitlyn hadn't planned to disclose any of it, the stone in her stomach, the lunches in the trash, the way she'd cried in the truck on moving day and then told her mother it was allergies. But it all came out anyway, and Ms. Byrne just listened, tapping her pen against her coffee mug. At her old school, Kaitlyn would have told Lenny first. Lenny would have made a joke and Kaitlyn would have laughed until her sides ached, and maybe that would have been enough. She still didn't know whether keeping quiet this week had been the right call or a mistake. Maybe both.

Ms. Byrne gave her a hall pass and the name of a girl in her science class, Christopher, who had moved here in fourth grade and still remembered what it was like. Kaitlyn folded the paper copy of the list and put it in her back pocket. In the hallway she passed the cafeteria, where the noise rolled out like a tide, and she stood there a moment with her hand on the door. Then she pushed it open and walked toward a table near the window.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks.
story:
The rink smelled like cold rubber and hot chocolate, and Andrew had the long bench by the boards to himself until Alvin and Cayson clattered down in their skates. Between the two of them they had one hockey card, one granola bar, and an argument.

"Marino is the best player in the league," Alvin said, tapping the card. "He's got the numbers."

"He's got one number," Cayson said. "That's not the same thing."

Andrew looked up at the rankings board that Ms. Esposito kept beside the snack bar, a transparent plastic sheet with the league scorers listed top to bottom. One column of numbers, tidy as anything, and a whole season squeezed inside it. He liked that about the board and also distrusted it. Ten games, six players, endless passes and whistles, and it all came down to a single digit beside each name.

"You're talking about batting average," Alvin said, because Marino's brother played triple-A baseball and Alvin followed the whole family like a soap opera. "Hits divided by at-bats. Two hundred hits, six hundred at-bats, three thirty-three. Clean and simple."

Andrew peeled off his gloves and did the arithmetic on the back of the ice-time tariff, the laminated sheet Ms. Esposito used to charge each team for its hour. "Wait," he said. "What about walks?"

"Walks aren't at-bats," Alvin said. "They don't go in."

"So the average gives him nothing for them." Andrew wrote it out. If Marino's brother had 40 hits in 120 at-bats, that came to .333, which looked brilliant on any board. But Andrew remembered watching the guy play on television once, taking pitch after pitch, leaning away from swings, drawing walks like it was a skill of its own. Andrew added 30 walks to the count and divided the 40 hits by 150 trips to the plate instead. The number sank below .270, but the times he reached base climbed way up. Same player, same season, different lens.

"That's backwards," Alvin said. "A guy who thrives on patience gets punished for it. He's on base more than anybody and the average says he's ordinary."

"Then the average is ordinary," Cayson said. "Not the player."

Ms. Esposito skated by with the ice-resurfacing schedule under her arm and paused at the board. "You three are going to melt my plastic sheet staring like that."

"Ms. Esposito," Andrew said, "when you rank the teams, do you use goals only?"

"Goals, then points, then wins," she said. "No single column ever tells the whole story. Ask any goalie with a bad record and a good team."

Andrew turned the tariff sheet over and drew two columns: one for hits, one for times on base. At the top he wrote Marino's brother's name, and under it, in careful print, "counted" and "not counted."

"New stat," he announced. "Every time you get on base, it counts."

Alvin took the pencil out of his hand and started filling in the first row.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file, called EXIF metadata.
story:
Alicia wanted one thing from the computer lab that Tuesday: a spot on the school news team, and Mr. Charles had said the spot would go to whoever brought him the best photo story by Friday. Dax had sent her three photos of the science fair from his phone, and she had planned to build her whole entry around them. She opened the first file on the lab computer, clicked "Get Info," and froze. Next to the picture was a tiny map, and the pin on it marked a street she recognized, because it was Dax's street.

"That's weird," she said, and Rosemary leaned over from the next computer.

"That's his house," Rosemary said. "Why does your laptop know where Dax lives?"

Alicia clicked through the file details and found numbers, a latitude and a longitude, written right there in the photo's information. "It says the exact GPS coordinates," she said slowly. "Like, exactly." She remembered Dax mentioning once that he'd taken the fair photos at school, but the pin said his street, so this had to be a different picture, taken at home before he'd left. She scrolled and found two more pins, one on his street and one at the school.

"It's in hidden data," Rosemary said, poking at the screen. "My cousin calls it EXIF metadata."

"That's a mouthful," Alicia said. She tested it the way she always tested things, by trying the opposite. She emailed a photo from the lab's old camera, which had no location services, and checked its details. No map. No pin. So the pin came from the phone. When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it writes the coordinates into the file, and anyone who opens the file can see them. Anyone at all. A stranger could do exactly what she had just done.

She thought about the negotiation she'd been running in her head all week, trading Dax free design help for his photos, and realized it didn't matter who sent a picture. Once it was shared, the hidden data went with it.

She called Dax over to the lab after last period. "Your photos are great," she told him, "but they're telling everyone your address. Turn off location services, then send them again."

Dax fumbled with his phone, resent the photos, and Alicia checked the new files. Clean. No pins anywhere.

"Creepy," Dax said. "Good creepy that we caught it."

"For my story," Alicia said, "this is the story." She dragged the clean photos into a folder labeled Friday, and hit save.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: Chiaroscuro, an Italian word meaning 'light-dark', is the name for using strong contrast between light and shadow to make shapes look solid.
story:
Alexander had sketched the same sphere six times before art class on Friday, and every time it looked like a flat gray pancake. Ms. Swampy wanted a sphere with a highlight, a shadow, and a cast shadow, and she had been clear that flat pancakes would not pass. Tonight the whole class was at the gallery for the evening sketch assignment, and Alexander only had until the bus left at eight.

He set up his pad in front of a still life with an orange, but his orange came out flat too. Beside him, Ilyes was already shading a wine bottle and looking smug about it. "It's the pressure of your pencil," Ilyes said. "Go darker."

Alexander pressed harder until his pencil tore a little hole in the paper. The sphere was darker, sure, but still flat as a coin. He rubbed the hole with his thumb and moved to another wall to escape Ilyes's helpfulness.

That was where he found the big painting, an old one with a candle glowing in it. A sphere sat on a table in the picture, and it looked so round Alexander felt he could pick it up. There was a bright spot where the candle's light hit it, a deep dark on the far side, and a long dark shape stretching across the table away from the light. He leaned close to the little label. "Chiaroscuro," he read aloud.

"That's the one," Robin said, appearing beside him with her own sketchbook. "It's an Italian word meaning light-dark. That's what they call it when a painter uses strong contrast between light and shadow to make shapes look solid." She tapped the label. "Caravaggio was famous for it."

Alexander stared at the painted sphere again. The painter hadn't made it round with soft, careful grays the way Alexander had been trying. The light side was almost white and the shadow side was almost black, and it was that contrast doing the work. He thought of his pancake sphere, all middle gray, and felt his ears go hot. Then he flipped to a new page and thought it through like a test: if the light came from the upper left, the highlight went upper left, the shadow lower right, and the cast shadow should stretch away from the light across the table. One simple rule, and he could point his pencil at it.

He drew fast, leaving the highlight as bare white paper, going assertive and black on the far side, then dragging the cast shadow out long. His hand cramped and he shook it to prolong his drawing time before the eight o'clock deadline. When Ms. Swampy came by, she picked up his pad and turned it toward the painting.

"Same trick," she said. "Chiaroscuro."

Alexander grinned and signed his name in the corner, black side down.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: The Gunnery camp, begun in 1861 by Connecticut schoolmaster Frederick W. Gunn, who led his students on a hike to a camp by the sea, is usually considered the first organized American summer camp.
story:
Grayson had never been away from home for a whole summer before, and his backpack was so stuffed that the zipper groaned when the counselor cinched it under the bus. Now he sat on a log beside Oceane and Willyam, watching the campfire crackle and spit while dew began to condense on his water bottle, beading up like tiny glass bubbles. The smoke kept changing direction, and every time it swung his way, the three of them scrambled sideways like startled rabbits.

"I heard there's a plaque on the lodge," Willyam said, poking a stick into the flames. "About the camp's history.mandatory reading for first-years, the counselor told me." Grayson sat up straight. A plaque meant a mystery, and mysteries were his favorite thing, even more than marshmallows. The camp director had already announced that tomorrow's orientation was mandatory too, but a secret metal plate bolted to a wall was far more interesting than any meeting.

He slipped away from the fire, flashlight bobbing, and found the lodge in the dark. Something rustled in the leaves, and he told himself it was only a rodent, probably a mouse, and kept walking. The plaque hung right beside the door, and his flashlight beam swept across the engraved letters. He read it twice, then three times, because the numbers felt impossible.

He ran back so fast he nearly kicked the fire ring. "Guess what! This isn't just some old camp," he panted. "The Gunnery camp started all the way back in 1861, and it was begun by a Connecticut schoolmaster named Frederick W. Gunn. He took his students on a hike to a camp by the sea!" He caught his breath. "It's usually considered the first organized American summer camp. Like, the first one ever. Camps are way older than I thought."

Oceane's marshmallow slid off her stick and landed in the dirt. "Older than my grandma?"

"Way older than your grandma." Willyam thrust his stick back into the flames. "Then that means we're part of, like, a chain. A hundred and sixty years of campers."

Grayson grabbed a fresh marshmallow and threaded it onto his stick, grinning into the fire. "First one to make a perfect golden one gets the top bunk."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: A cow's stomach has four compartments, and the first, the rumen, holds microbes that help break down tough grass the cow later brings back up and chews again as cud.
story:
The bus smelled like hay and peanut butter sandwiches, and it would reach Hollis Farm in twenty minutes, which meant Leo had twenty minutes to win the bet. Louis had made it in the third row that morning: five dollars said nobody in the class could explain what a cow was doing when it chewed with nothing in its mouth. Mr. Vargas, who overheard everything from the front seat, had added the deadline. "You have until the gate opens," he said. "No phones."

Leo leaned over the seat to Maximiliano. "It's not swallowing air. Animals don't waste energy like that." Maximiliano suggested the cow was nervous, like a kid before an audition, but Leo shook his head. "Cows do it all day. Nervous chewing fluctuates. It comes and goes. This looks like a habit."

He closed his eyes and went back to Tuesday, to the video Mr. Vargas had played with the sound off while he graded papers. Leo had been half listening, doodling a dinosaur, when the screen showed a diagram of a cow cut open like a drawer. Four compartments, the caption said, stacked like rooms in a strange house. The first room had a name. Leo had copied it on his hand in pen and washed it off the same night.

"Rumen," he said out loud. Louis turned around. "What?" "The first compartment. It's called the rumen." Maximiliano frowned. "A cow has compartments?" "Four of them. The rumen is first, and it holds microbes, little living things, that break down tough grass. Then the cow brings that grass back up and chews it again." Louis laughed. "Chews it twice? That's disgusting." "It's called cud," Leo said, though he wasn't sure of that part until the bus stopped at the gate and Mr. Vargas called time.

The farmer let them into the paddock, where a brown cow stood at the fence, jaw working in slow circles, no grass anywhere near her mouth. Louis pointed. "Okay, genius. Prove it." Leo picked a tuft of the tough, pale grass growing along the fence line, the kind the farmer said the field had given them for free after years of impoverished soil, and held it near the cow's nose. She swallowed it, and her jaw went still for a long moment, and then the circles started again, unhurried, like she had all afternoon. Mr. Vargas wrote something in his notebook and didn't say what. Louis dug into his pocket, pulled out a crumpled five, and slapped it into Leo's palm. "She ate your grass and started chewing it twice. I hate that I understand this." The cow swallowed, waited, and chewed.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In February 2015 a photo of a dress went viral because some people saw it as blue and black and others as white and gold; the real dress was blue and black.
story:
Victor slid his phone across the dinner table until it stopped beside his father's fork. "What color is that dress?" he asked. His father squinted at the screen. "White and gold, obviously." His mother leaned over from the sink, dried her hands, and frowned. "It's blue and black. Are you two playing a trick on me?" Victor's little sister grabbed the phone and shouted "Gold!" before anyone could stop her. Victor looked around the table at three people staring at the exact same picture and seeing two completely different dresses. That was the problem. He had to find out who was wrong, and how.

He thought about lunch, when Liana had held up her phone in the cafeteria and the table had split almost in half. Etienne had slammed his milk carton down and said the photo was everywhere, that it had gone viral back in February 2015, and that the whole internet was fighting about it. Etienne's older sister had looked it up and reported, smugly, that the real dress was blue and black. Victor had assumed Etienne's sister was wrong or teasing, because to Victor the dress was clearly white and gold, and a picture couldn't just lie.

So at dinner he ran a test. He took the phone back, cleared his throat, and showed the photo to each person one at a time, alone, so nobody could influence anybody else's answer. His father said white and gold again. His mother said blue and black again. His sister said gold, then blue, then got upset and put her head down on the table. Victor wrote the answers on a napkin like a scientist. The results did not change. The photo itself, he realized, was the strange part, not the people.

His mother sat down and put an arm around his sulking sister, showing a kind of compassion that made Victor feel bad about treating the argument like a game. "Maybe," she said, "we could collaborate instead of fight. Draw what you see, and compare." His sister lifted her head. His father said, "Fine, but I'm drawing gold." Victor pulled out the crayon box, thinking of how influential that one little photo must have been, to make millions of strangers argue exactly like his family was arguing now. "Blue and black," he said, and held up a crayon to prove it.

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: A quotation used as evidence must be copied word for word, with the same spelling and punctuation, inside quotation marks.
story:
Michael sat cross-legged in the reading nook, the cushion in the window seat pressing into his knees, with his notebook open to a page titled THEME. The book was "Where the Red Fern Grows," and he was pretty sure the theme was love and loyalty, because Old Dan and Little Ann stuck together no matter what. The problem was that Mr. Hoang had said a theme needed evidence, a quotation copied exactly from the text, and Michael wanted to write it before dinner.

He remembered a line near the end, something like "a part of my heart died with them," and he wrote it down, feeling pleased. Then he paused. Was that really how it went? He flipped backward through the pages, hunting. It made him think of last summer, when he had told Emerson that a granola bar was healthy and Emerson had turned the label around and shown him the carbohydrate count, which was significant, higher than in a candy bar. "You assumed it was healthy," Emerson had said. "Assuming gets you in trouble." Michael had never forgotten that, and now he had a small suspicious feeling about his quotation too.

He found the page. His pencil hovered. He had written "a part of my heart," but the book said "a part of my life." And it wasn't "died with them," it was "died that night." Two words wrong, and his quotation marks were around words the author had never written. So that was the rule, he realized: a quotation used as evidence must be copied word for word, with the same spelling and punctuation, inside quotation marks. He erased his line and wrote the real one, checking each word against the page like a detective comparing handwriting.

He copied the quotation onto a card for Mr. Hoang, then held it beside the book one last time, letter by letter, comma by comma. "You're mine now," he told the card, and slid it into his binder.

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: Mediators usually start by setting ground rules, such as one person speaks at a time and no name-calling, which both sides agree to before talking.
story:
Levi had promised his grandpa that he would keep the peace at the house while Grandpa napped in his rocking chair, and for ten whole minutes it had gone well. Then Soleil and Lya started arguing about who had lost the badminton birdie, and it got loud fast.

"You always hog the racket!" Lya shouted.

"You knocked it into the hydrangeas on purpose!" Soleil shouted back, and then they were both talking at once, louder and louder, until Levi could not understand a single word from either of them. He tried being the referee, which mostly meant yelling "Soleil started it" and then feeling bad, because Lya's face went stormy and the argument restarted twice from the beginning, like a song stuck on the same verse. It even followed them inside, where they argued over who got the good cushion on the porch swing.

While they glared at each other, Levi slipped into Grandpa's study and pulled a dusty paperback off the shelf, something about settling disputes. He flipped until he found a chapter that made him grin. "Hey," he called, waving the book. "It says here a mediator sets ground rules first." The word felt important in his mouth, like a password. "One person speaks at a time, and no name-calling. Both sides have to agree before you even start talking."

"Fine," Soleil muttered.

"Fine," Lya muttered.

Levi pulled two chairs to face each other on the porch and squeezed a third one in the middle to accommodate all three of them, though his knees bumped both friends at once. "Rule one, Lya talks first. Soleil, you're on mute." He pointed at Soleil like a judge, which was extremely satisfying. Lya explained that the birdie had been sitting on the porch rail, not in the hydrangeas, and Soleil, unmuted, admitted he had batted it off the rail to be funny and lost it in the petunias. They stared at each other.

"We are the most incompetent birdie players in the history of the sport," Soleil said solemnly, "and I say we take a census of the petunias."

"Motion carried," Lya said, already kneeling in the flowerbed.

They found the birdie in under a minute, along with a spoon, a golf ball, and one of Grandpa's slippers. "Case closed," Levi announced, and both friends pelted him with petunia petals until he fell off his chair, laughing.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish generally uses "ser" for lasting traits and "estar" for temporary states: "Mi hermano es alto" means he is tall, while "Mi hermano está cansado" means he is tired.
story:
"Two minutes left," Mr. Delgado called, and Maeva's pencil hovered over the blank line.

Tomorrow was the speaking quiz: describe your family and pets in full Spanish sentences. She had her dog, her mothers, and her little brother, and she could say their names, their sizes, even that the dog was ridiculous. What she could not remember was when to use "es" and when to use "estar."

Memphis leaned over from the next desk. "My grandpa keeps fish. If I win the practice game, you have to help me film them for my database. I'm generating a whole catalog of fish colors."

"You can't film a fish being blue," Ephraim said. "It just is blue."

That word snagged in Maeva's head. Is. Her brother is tall. That was always true, or at least true for years. She wrote "Mi hermano es alto." Then she thought about him after soccer practice, sprawled on the couch, and wrote "Mi hermano está cansado." Tired was not forever. Nobody was born tired.

She looked at the two sentences side by side. Lasting thing got "es." Passing thing got "estar." She tested it with the dog. "Mi perro es pequeno," because he would be small his whole life. But if he rolled in mud, "Mi perro está sucio." She flipped through her notebook, hunting for every sentence she'd written that week, and found the mistake: "Mi hermano es cansado." She had accidentally said her brother was permanently, forever tired.

"Is that right?" Memphis asked, peering at the page.

"No, and it explains why Mr. Delgado laughed on Tuesday." Maeva crossed out "es" and wrote "está." She remembered being embarrassed then, impulsive enough to blurt that the worksheet was wrong instead of checking her own word. She'd spent two days thinking the teacher was picking on her, when really she'd sentenced her brother to eternal sleepiness.

"Pencils down," Mr. Delgado said. "Read one sentence aloud."

Memphis went first, fast and confident, about his grandfather's fish. He got stuck, tried "estar" where "es" belonged, and chewed his lip. "Can I change my answer?" he asked.

"You just did," Mr. Delgado said.

Maeva raised her hand and read, "Mi hermano está cansado." Then, for good measure, "pero es alto."

"Very good," Mr. Delgado said, and wrote something in his grade book.

At recess, Memphis shoved his phone toward the fish tank in the back of the room. "Deal's a deal. Say something about the fish in Spanish."

Maeva looked at the fat orange one circling the castle. "El pez es naranja," she said. "Y está hambriento. Probably."

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: British economist Alfred Marshall popularized the supply-and-demand diagram, with its two crossing curves, in his 1890 book Principles of Economics.
story:
Jessica spread her homework across Grandpa's kitchen table, which was a mistake, because the table was already covered with seed catalogs and a radiator valve Grandpa had taken apart. "The question is who first made the supply-and-demand curves famous," she said. "Not just what they are. Who made them famous." Liliane, who had come over because her own house had no snacks, looked at the two crossing lines Jessica had drawn and said they looked like scissors. "Scissors that decide how much strawberries cost," Jessica said. "Cheap in summer, expensive in winter."

That was the part she had to explain, and she had a plan. Grandpa's neighbor Ms. Choi kept a little notebook of every price she paid at the market, going back years, because she did not trust stores to be honest about sales. Jessica and Liliane knocked on her door and asked if she'd ever written down strawberry prices. Ms. Choi found the notebook, and there it was, winter after winter, the same numbers climbing like something on a ladder. In summer the prices dropped so low they almost fell off the page. "See," Jessica whispered. "Lots of strawberries in summer, not many in winter. The price follows."

Back at the table, Grandpa was wrapping foam around the pipes under the sink, muttering that he would not have burst pipes just because the weather turned. He paused over her drawing of the crossing curves. "That looks like something out of an old book," he said, and pointed at the shelf behind him, where a fat faded economics text had been sitting so long it was nearly part of the wall. Jessica hauled it down. It was a copy of Principles of Economics, by a British economist named Alfred Marshall, and there on the page were her scissors, the two curves crossing exactly the way she'd drawn them. She checked the front. 1890.

"That's him," Jessica said. "Alfred Marshall. 1890. He's the one who made the diagram famous." Liliane, wearing her T-shirt with the extinct dinosaur on it that said THINK ABOUT IT, leaned over her shoulder. "So your homework answer was in Grandpa's house the whole time." "It was in the house the whole time," Jessica agreed. "I was just the one who had to dig it out."

She wrote her paragraph: strawberries cheap in summer because there were so many, expensive in winter because there weren't, the price sitting wherever the two curves crossed. Then, at the bottom, she added the date and the name, and underlined them. Ms. Choi's notebook went back next door, minus one page, which Ms. Choi had torn out herself and handed over. "Evidence," she said. Jessica taped it into her notebook, right beside the two crossing curves.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: A hook is the opening line that grabs attention, such as a question, a surprising fact or a very short story.
story:
Alexia sat in the third row of the cafeteria-turned-debate-hall, watching a boy named Merrick stand at the podium and say, "Today I will talk about school uniforms." By his second sentence, the judge was writing something in her notebook, and the girl beside Alexia was drawing a cat on her program. Alexia felt her stomach tighten, because her own two-minute speech was next, and she was planning to open the exact same way.

She grabbed her friend Kellen's sleeve. "What just happened to that room?" she whispered.

"You mean how everybody's brains floated out the window?" Kellen whispered back.

Alexia thought about it while the judge scored Merrick's round. His points were fine, actually. Uniforms save money if a family is frugal, they cut down on morning arguments, and they let students focus on learning instead of labels. It was the first line that failed, and she could see the pattern: when he said "Today I will talk about," the audience's eyes went glassy, like a spell that made everything he said afterward invisible. There had to be a way to break the spell. She looked at her notes, crossed out her first sentence, and wrote a single question above it.

"Alexia, Room Two, you're up," Ms. Rodríguez called from the doorway.

Alexia walked to the podium, took a breath, and said, "Did you know a shark can replace its teeth forever, but you only get two sets?" The cat-drawing girl looked up. The judge's pen stopped. Alexia pushed on before the magic could fade. "Imagine if we only got two ideas in our whole lives. We'd have to spend them carefully. That's why I'm asking you to spend two minutes on my three points." She gave them, one by one, and closed by returning to the shark, which she decided was the part people would remember on the bus ride home.

Afterward, Kellen caught her in the hallway. "A shark? At a debate about democracy?"

"Ms. Rodríguez calls it a hook," Alexia said. "A question, a surprising fact, or a very short story." She held up her notes, where she had written HOOK in giant letters and underlined it twice. "Next time I'm monitoring the whole front row while I talk, to see if their eyes stay on me."

"Better than a cat," said Kellen.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The crowd 'wave' became known worldwide at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, so many English speakers outside North America call it the Mexican wave.
story:
Carson had exactly one half of soccer left to start a wave in Mr. Campbell-Brown's living room, and so far nobody was standing up but him.

The whole crowd was packed in there because the big screen in Mr. Campbell-Brown's basement was the biggest on the street. Carson's dad brought chips, Elie brought a library book about jet engines that he kept reading during throw-ins, and Nikolas brought his cousin, who was visiting from England and wore a scarf indoors even though it was June. On the screen, the stadium rippled with a wave, thousands of people standing and sitting in one smooth roll all the way around the bowl. "They call that the Mexican wave," the cousin said, pointing with a chip. "It went worldwide at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico. That's what everyone back home says, anyway."

"It's just the wave," Nikolas said. But Carson was staring at the screen, not arguing. He'd tried three times already to start one in the basement and each time it collapsed after Elie, who was too deep in his book about turbine blades to notice a human rising beside him. Now he studied the stadium crowd instead. The wave wasn't started by everybody at once; the camera showed one section standing a beat before the next, like dominoes that had to be spaced out. Maybe his wave kept dying because everyone shot up together and there was nothing to follow. If he could calibrate the timing, one person, then the next, then the next, maybe it would roll. Elie glanced up from his book. "Are you counting?" he asked. "Yes," Carson said. "Watch the screen with me. Tell me how long between rows."

The scoreboard clock showed ten minutes to halftime, which was the deadline, because at halftime everybody would go up for cake and never come back down in the same order. Carson moved people like a coach. He put Nikolas at the far end of the couch, his dad behind the snacks, the cousin by the door. "When I stand, you wait until I'm fully up, then go. Not before." "This seems like a legitimate plan," the cousin admitted, "for a boy with chip grease on his shirt." Elie closed his book on his thumb to hold his page, which Carson decided to take as loyalty.

When the home team nearly scored, the whole basement leaned forward, and that was the moment Carson stood. Nikolas rose a beat later, then the dad, then Elie, and the cousin flung his scarf overhead like a flag. From the top of the stairs, Mr. Campbell-Brown looked down at all of them bobbing in sequence and called out, "Is that a Mexican wave in my house?" "It's the wave," Carson said, already sitting, already counting toward the next one.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: Where strawberries ripen outdoors in early summer, a flood of local berries raises the supply all at once, which usually pushes their price down.
story:
Zoe stood in line at the bank behind Anson, holding the shoebox of quarters her class had collected for the strawberry stand they were planning at the spring fair. The shoebox had a drawing of a strawberry on it, done in orange crayon, because Anson had used up the red one on something he would not recount in detail.

"Here's what I don't get," Anson said, for the third time. "In March I bought strawberries with my mom and they cost four dollars a basket. At the market last weekend, same basket, two dollars. Half. Same berries. Who decided that?"

"Nobody decided," Zoe said. The line moved forward one person. An obstinate old man at the counter was arguing about a coin roll, so they had time.

"Somebody had to decide. There's a price sticker."

Zoe thought about it while a pigeon outside walked along the ledge, studying the lichen on the stone like it was lunch. Lots of things worked like the pigeon: you couldn't see the rule, only the walking. In March the berries came from somewhere far away and there weren't many. Then, near the end of June, every farm around had berries ripe outdoors all at once, the whole lot of them showing up in one great flood, and the price dropped. It wasn't a decision. It was like a bucket. Pour more in and the level changes whether the bucket agrees or not.

"Try this," she said. "Say you're the only kid at school with a strawberry basket, and everybody wants one. What happens to your price?"

"I charge four dollars. Maybe five for Hadassah, she's rich."

"Now every kid at school has a basket. Same number of buyers, tons more baskets."

Anson frowned at the shoebox. "Then I'd have to go cheap or eat them all myself." He looked briefly haunted by the math. "So in June there's just more of them, all at once, from around here?"

"That's supply," Zoe said. "When the supply jumps like that, the price usually falls. That's why summer berries cost half of what they did in March."

They reached the counter, where Mr. Chatterjee, their neighbour from four doors down, waited with the patience of a man who had already dealt with the coin roll. Zoe slid the box over and announced the deposit: two hundred and six dollars, plus one bus token Anson had contributed by mistake.

"For the strawberry stand," she said. "We're selling in June, when berries are cheap. Anson wanted March."

"March," Anson confirmed, "was before we understood buckets."

Mr. Chatterjee counted the quarters, wrote the receipt, and slid back the token. "For the bus," he said. "It has no supply problem."

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Many home ovens run hotter or cooler than the temperature on the dial, which an oven thermometer placed inside can reveal.
story:
Nathan cracked two eggs into the bowl and fished out a sliver of shell with his fingertip. The campsite's little kitchen shed had one small oven, a dented dial, and a laminated recipe card that Ms. Joseph had handed him that morning. "Blueberry muffins, start to finish, all yours," she had said, and then she had walked off toward the lake, leaving him with a mixing bowl and a clock that said ten past nine.

His friend Eshal sat on the counter, supposedly reading but mostly watching. "You preheated already, right? It says preheat first."

"Done," Nathan said. He had turned the dial to three seventy-five before he measured the flour, exactly the way the card ordered it. He folded in the blueberries, spooned batter into twelve cups, and slid the pan in. Twenty minutes, the card said.

At fourteen minutes, the smell came. Not warm-blueberry smell. Burnt smell, abrupt and sharp, filling the whole shed. Nathan pulled the pan out with a dish towel and stared at twelve muffin tops gone dark brown, nearly black at the edges. "That's wrong," he said. "I set it right. Three seventy-five."

"Maybe the recipe's wrong," Eshal said.

"It can't be. Ms. Joseph's made these a hundred times." Nathan looked at the dial, then at the burnt pan, then at the dial again. He remembered something his grandfather had grumbled about at Christmas, that his own oven burned everything no matter what the dial said, that nobody could trust the number. A hidden cause, he thought. Something you couldn't see from the outside.

He hunted through the drawer of mismatched tools and found a small round thermometer with a metal probe, the kind you hang from an oven rack. He clipped it inside, shut the door, and waited. When he peeked again, the thermometer read four hundred and twenty-five, a full fifty degrees hotter than the dial claimed.

"Look at that," Eshal said, leaning over his shoulder. "The dial's lying."

"Many home ovens run hotter or cooler than the temperature on the dial," Nathan said slowly, reading the little card stapled to the thermometer's case. "But a thermometer inside shows the truth." So he turned the dial down until the needle settled near three seventy-five, mixed a fresh batch, and slid it in. Lichen-pale compared to the first pan, the new muffins came out at nineteen minutes, golden and domed.

Ms. Joseph came back from the lake, sniffed the air, and raised an eyebrow at the blackened pan sitting in the sink.

"The oven runs hot," Nathan said, holding up the thermometer like a trophy. "Try one."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word Inuit means 'the people' in the Inuktitut language, and one person is called an Inuk.
story:
Eli held the glue stick over the poster board and tried to look like he knew what he was doing. Penny's kitchen table was covered with photographs: her grandmother in a parka stitched with white and blue trim, a village of small houses at the edge of grey water, and a snapshot of Penny herself at age four, scowling at a bowl of something nutritious that she clearly had not wanted to eat.

"The caption under this one is wrong," Penny said, tapping a photo of her grandmother standing alone on the ice. Eli leaned in and scrutinized the typed label. "An Inuit woman, 1978," it read. He couldn't see anything wrong with it.

"She's my grandmother," Penny said. "One person."

"So?"

"So I asked my mom this morning and she looked it up, and then my grandpa called from Ottawa and told me the whole thing twice." Penny pulled a napkin from the stack her mother had left beside the seal soup, drew a line down the middle, and wrote Inuit on the left side. "Inuit means 'the people.' In Inuktitut. All of them together, the people." On the right side she wrote Inuk and underlined it so hard the pen nearly went through. "One person is an Inuk."

Eli stared at the two words. Same first four letters, different endings, like the word knew whether it was talking about one or many. He tested it out loud. "Your grandmother is an Inuk. Your whole family is Inuit."

"Now you sound like my grandpa," Penny said, and grinned.

They fixed the caption together, and Eli noticed something else. Half the photos showed groups, half showed one person, and every label Penny had typed used the same word for both. He got the correction tape and they went through all twelve, one by one, arguing about whether a photo of two cousins counted as people or a person. They decided on people. Penny's little brother offered to eat the glue stick and was removed from the table.
