Under the photo of the village, Penny typed a new line about how her grandfather had left the north for a job down south during the recession, when the fishing work dried up, and how her grandmother had stayed. "He says he was homesick the whole time," she added. "He calls it a word I can't spell."

Eli read the finished poster from top to bottom. "You should put the soup recipe on the back."

"It's seal."

"Put it on the back," he said again, and Penny, still grinning, reached for the napkin stack.

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: When two singers hold nearly but not exactly the same pitch, the sound pulses with a wobble called beats, which slows and disappears as they match.
story:
The choir room smelled like old risers and floor wax, and Addison stood in the alto row trying to hold her note while the sopranos floated above her. Mr. Lewandowski lifted both hands. "Second measure, altos only," he said, and Addison sang with Emy-Jade beside her. Something was wrong. Their two voices didn't blend; the note wobbled, like a flag flapping in slow motion, faster when they started and slower near the end. Addison's face went hot. Maybe the wobble was her fault. Maybe everyone could hear it.

She remembered her very first rehearsal in September, when she had hidden behind Alexander and only mouthed the words, afraid to let one sound out of her mouth. That had been a small quiet rebellion, and Mr. Lewandowski had caught it anyway, tapping the empty air where her voice should have been. She had promised herself she would never hide again. So now, standing in the same spot, she refused to shrink. She had to figure this out out loud.

During the break she pulled Emy-Jade behind the risers, past the poster about not storing flammable things in the boiler room. "Hold the F with me," Addison whispered. They sang. The wobble came back, pulsing like a heartbeat in the air. Then Addison had an idea. "Sing it again, but creep your note up a tiny bit." Emy-Jade did. Slowly, the pulsing slowed. When their notes finally locked together, the wobble disappeared and the sound turned into one smooth thread.

"Mr. Lewandowski called that beats once," Alexander said, popping around the corner. "When two singers are nearly but not exactly on the same pitch, you get that wobble, and it slows and vanishes as they match."

"We were almost the same," Emy-Jade said, grinning. "Almost."

"Almost isn't blending," Addison said. She grabbed Emy-Jade's hand and marched back to the risers. When Mr. Lewandowski raised his hands for the whole choir, the two parts fit together, and for the first time Addison heard her line integrate with the sopranos instead of fighting them. "Again, from the top," he called, and Addison drew her breath.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Complementary colors sit opposite each other on the color wheel, such as red and green, and mixing two complementary paints produces a dull brown or gray.
story:
Hunter squinted at his painting of a sunset over the camp lake and frowned. He had mixed what should have been a blazing orange sky, but every time he added red to the greenish water below the horizon, the two paints smudged together into a muddy brown smear. He had painted over that same corner four times already.

"You look like you lost a wrestling match with your palette," said Nikhil, pulling a stool up beside him in the art shed. The fans in the window pushed warm pine smell through the room, and paint drips dotted the old plank floor.

"Watch this." Hunter dabbed red onto the green water. Where the brushes met, the color went dull, almost gray-brown, like wet dirt. "See? Every sunset I try turns into mud."

Arnav leaned over from the next easel. He was the veteran of this craft program, three summers of it, and his canvas had an actual lake that looked like water. "Let me see your colors," he said. He pointed at the poster Ms. Zhang kept tacked above the supply shelf, a circle with red, yellow, blue, green, orange and purple arranged around it. "Red and green sit opposite each other on that wheel. They're complementary colors."

"Like a compliment?" Nikhil asked.

"Opposite," Arnav said. "And mixing two complementary paints gives you a dull brown or gray." He tapped the muddy patch on Hunter's canvas. "That's your mud right there."

Hunter stared at the wheel. Red across from green, purple across from yellow. He tested it, squeezing a dot of purple and a dot of yellow onto a scrap of cardboard and swirling them with a brush tip. Dull gray-brown, just like his sunset. Yellow and blue, which sat next to each other, made a clean green instead. It was the position on the wheel that mattered, not the paints themselves.

"So I keep my red sky and my green water away from each other," Hunter said slowly. He let the red hillside dry completely before he touched the water line again, and this time he dragged the brush upward instead of sideways, so the wet edges never crossed. Nikhil cooperated by holding the canvas steady while Hunter worked the horizon.

By the end of the session, the sunset glowed orange and red above a lake that shone green and blue, with a clean edge between them. Ms. Zhang walked past, stopped, and whistled. "That's a versatile little painting," she said. "Goes from fire to water without a single muddy spot."

"I have opposites to thank," Hunter said, and signed his name in the corner with the smallest brush he could find.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: In his book Opticks, first published in 1704, Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle, an early form of the color wheel.
story:
Aaron wanted his color wheel to be the best project at Camp Birchwood, but the paint kept going on in the wrong order, and he couldn't figure out why. He had a vague memory of a poster from art class, red next to orange next to yellow, but after that the whole circle turned into mud in his head. Across the picnic table, Darcy was gluing together a wooden propeller for a rubber-band plane, and Simone was lettering a sign that said MESS HALL FOOD: MOSTLY HARMLESS.

"You're overthinking it," Darcy said. "It's just a circle. Paint it any way you want. Art doesn't need rules."

"Then why does mine look wrong and the poster look right?" Aaron said. He turned his paper over and started again. "Somebody figured out the order. Somebody had to be first."

Ms. Abdi, the crafts instructor, was restocking the paint shelf, and Aaron almost asked her, then stopped. She would just tell him the answer, and he wanted to find it himself. So that evening he wrote a letter to the camp librarian and left it in the return box.

Dear Librarian, it began. Who made the first color wheel? Not a modern one, the first one. Please don't just say "an artist." I want a name. Aaron.

The next morning a note was waiting in his mailbox, folded into a square the size of a gum wrapper. Isaac Newton, it said. In his book Opticks, first published in 1704, he arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle. So it wasn't an artist at all. Aaron read it three times.

"A scientist," he told Simone at breakfast. "Newton. In his book Opticks, published in 1704, he arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle. That was an early form of the color wheel."

"So the spectrum order, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, that's the order," Simone said, tearing her toast. "You kept starting with blue."

At the crafts table Aaron cut out a fresh paper circle. He drew a line to isolate each wedge so the colors wouldn't run together, then painted them in spectrum order. When he spun the wheel on a pencil point, the colors blurred toward white. Darcy leaned over from her propeller, watched the spin, and frowned.

"Okay," she said. "Maybe I was wrong about the rules thing." She picked up a marker and wrote NEWTON, 1704 in small letters at the bottom of her plane's wing. "If he's good enough for paint, he's good enough for flying."

She wound the rubber band and let go, and the plane looped twice over the picnic table and landed in the glue.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it.
story:
Hailey flipped her word list over for the tenth time that morning, and the paper had gone soft at the corners from all her rereading. "Rhinoceros. Rendezvous. Rhythm." She whispered them in order, but when she covered the page and tried to spell rhythm from memory, her mind went blank, like the word had slipped out a side door.

"Stop that," said Jax, sliding into the desk beside her. "You're going to irritate your eyes staring at that thing." He pointed at the list. "Quizzing beats rereading anyway. My mom read about it. A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it. That's why she drills me with flashcards instead of letting me just look at them."

Hailey frowned. "But rereading feels like studying."

"That's the trap," Jax said. "It feels good because it's easy." He held out his hand. "Give me the list. If you get one wrong, I'll say it again, and you try it cold."

All week, Jax had quizzed her at lunch, at recess, and once on the bus while the driver shouted for everyone to sit down. When she misspelled rendezvous four times in a row, she blamed him. "You have a bias against me," she said. "You keep picking the hard ones on purpose."

"I pick the ones you miss," Jax said. "That's not bias, that's logical." He was right, and she knew it, so she spelled it until the z and the double s stopped hiding from her.

On the day of the spelling bee, Ms. Lindqvist stood at the front of the classroom with the word cards. Kurt went first and sat down fast after stumbling on "sincerely." Then it was Hailey's turn.

"Rendezvous," said Ms. Lindqvist.

Hailey closed her eyes. She didn't picture the list, because the list had never really gone in. She pictured Jax on the bus, saying "you dropped the z again," and herself writing it in the fog on the window.

"R-E-N-D-E-Z-V-O-U-S," she said. "Rendezvous."

"Correct," said Ms. Lindqvist, and Hailey heard Jax's sneakers squeak as he bounced in his seat.

"Rhythm," said Ms. Lindqvist next, and Hailey almost laughed, because this was the word that had started everything, the one that kept escaping through the side door.

"R-H-Y-T-H-M," she said. She opened her eyes and looked at Jax.

"Told you," he mouthed, and held up the worn word list like a trophy.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When the price of one good rises, many buyers switch to a substitute, a similar good that does the same job, so demand for the substitute goes up.
story:
Edouard stood in front of the chip shelf with his mother's list in his hand, and one item was circled twice: Golden Ridge tortilla chips, family size. The tag said $6.49. Last month it had been $3.99, because Edouard had memorized it, the way some kids memorized batting averages.

"That can't be right," he said to Baylee, who had tagged along because her own mother was somewhere in the frozen aisle and Baylee got bored near the freezers.

"Scan it," Baylee said, pointing at the price checker mounted on the end cap. Edouard scanned the bag. The machine agreed with the tag, which he felt was a little smug of it.

"So we don't get them," he said. He picked up the store brand instead, Hilltop tortilla chips, which cost $2.79. "These are the substitute. Same job, basically."

"Basically," said Baylee, with heavy skepticism. "They taste like drywall."

"You'd eat drywall if it was salted," Edouard said, dropping two bags in the cart. He noticed the Golden Ridge shelf was fully stocked, untouched rows of $6.49 chips, while the Hilltop section had a ragged gap in the middle where shoppers had clearly been reaching in. He filed that away.

At the register, Ms. Munro, his neighbor, was ahead of them in line, and in her basket sat three bags of Hilltop chips. "They jacked up the price of the other kind," she said to the cashier, not sadly at all. "So now I'm on these. I can consume an entire bag during one episode of anything."

Edouard leaned toward Baylee and lowered his voice. "See? When the Golden Ridge price went up, everyone switched. That's why the Hilltop shelf is half empty. More people want it now."

"That's one neighbor," said Baylee. "Your evidence is one neighbor."

Edouard walked back to the snack aisle alone, counting. Eleven bags of Hilltop left, out of what looked like a full row that morning, judging by the shelf labels. Sixty-two bags of Golden Ridge, sitting there like expensive wall decorations. He took a photo of both shelves as proof, then texted it to Baylee with one word: "gullible," by which he meant she was being stubborn, though he conceded it might not be the exact right word.

Back at the cart, Baylee looked at the photo for a long moment. "Fine," she said, tearing open a bag of Hilltop before they'd even paid for it. She chewed, frowned, chewed again. "Okay, it's not drywall."

"Told you," said Edouard, and he put a third bag in the cart.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: Reflected light is light bouncing back from the table onto a sphere's shadow side; it is lighter than the core shadow but always darker than the lit side.
story:
Blake set a golf ball on the picnic table in the backyard and crouched until his eyes were level with it. The afternoon sun came from the left, hard and steady, which was lucky because Ms. Sutherland had made a real object mandatory for the art assignment. No drawing from memory. "You copy what you imagine instead of what you see," she had said, and Blake knew she was right, because last week he had drawn an apple with a shadow shaped like a banana and turned it in anyway.

Trystan dropped onto the bench across from him with his own sketchbook. "I hate this project," he announced. "My hand keeps accelerating ahead of my eyes. I finish the whole sphere before I've looked at it."

"That's because you're drawing with hormones instead of patience," Kenzo said, climbing over the fence, which was his usual entrance. "My sister says that about me when I eat too fast."

Blake ignored them both. He had already found the bright spot on the ball where the sun hit it straight on, and the fat dark shadow the ball threw sideways across the table. That part made sense. What confused him was the shadow side of the ball itself. The top of that side was deep gray, almost black, but near the bottom, where the ball touched the table, something strange happened. It got lighter again. He squinted at it for a long moment, then shaded the lower edge of his sphere nearly white, because lighter had to mean lighter, right?

He held up the drawing. "Huh."

"That looks wrong," Trystan said at once. "Like the ball has two suns."

"Two lamps," Kenzo said. "One on the left, one underneath. Ms. Sutherland would fail that."

Blake looked from his drawing to the real ball and back. He had copied what was there, sort of, but he had pushed it too far. The bottom edge of the shadow side was lighter, true, but only a little, and it was still way darker than the sunny side. He remembered, suddenly, a page in the art book he'd left open on his bed last night, and the phrase came back to him. "Reflected light," he said slowly. "That's what that lighter bit is called."

"Reflected off what?" Trystan asked.

"The table. It bounces back up onto the ball." Blake took his eraser and knocked the white down to a soft middle gray, then darkened the band above it so the dark part stayed the darkest of all. He set the drawing beside the ball and looked again. One sun. One light, one shadow, one pale whisper at the bottom where the table gave a little back.

Trystan leaned over and studied it. "Okay, that's better than mine. Don't tell Kenzo I said that."

Kenzo was already reaching for Blake's pencil. "Trade me balls," he said. "Mine looks like a planet with a ring."

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: A short silent pause in place of 'um' or 'uh' makes a speaker sound more confident and gives listeners time to take in the point.
story:
Gabrielle stood at the front of Room 12 with her note cards shaking like a nervous rodent trying to escape her hands. Her speech was about why the school should get a second water fountain, and it had a proper opening hook, three solid points, and a closing line Mr. Haddad would love. The problem was that every third word out of her mouth was "um."

"Twenty-two," said Micah, clicking a pen each time she said it. "Twenty-three. Gabi, you said 'um' more times than you said 'water.'"

"That is not possible," Gabrielle said. "Um." Micah clicked the pen again and grinned.

Alexandre slid his chair around so she could practice on him too, because apparently one victim was not enough. On her second run she tried to catch herself, but the "ums" just changed shape. "Uh" showed up. Then "like." Then a horrible new sound that was half word, half squeak.

"Try this," Alexandre said. "When you feel an 'um' coming, just stop. Say nothing. Just for a second."

Gabrielle squinted at him. "Stop? In the middle? That sounds like my brain is buffering."

"Trust me," he said. "I watched a documentary about penguins. The narrator paused all the time and he sounded like he owned the world."

She gave it one more run, and it felt strange, like stepping off a curb she hadn't known was there. Every time the next word refused to come, she closed her mouth and waited instead of filling the gap. Micah's pen stayed quiet. At the end he counted his tally marks, looked betrayed, and reported, "Four. Only four. I had a whole system."

"Where did the rest go?" Gabrielle asked.

"You replaced them with silences," Alexandre said, tapping the desk at each spot she had paused. "Right there. And there. Honestly, it sounded better. Like you were letting the point sink in before the next one."

Gabrielle wasn't sure she believed him. Maybe Micah's counting was random and she had simply gotten lucky, so she decided to test it properly. She did one more practice run pausing on purpose, then one final run going back to her old ways. Micah's pen clicked twenty-nine times on the last one, and by the end Alexandre was laughing so hard he nearly fell out of his chair.

Speech day arrived. Mr. Haddad called her name, and Gabrielle walked up determined not to expose her nervousness to the whole class. She opened with her hook, which was the fact that the line at the one water fountain once made her miss four minutes of dodgeball. Silence where the "um" wanted to be. Point one. Silence again, steady as a held breath. Point two, point three, closing line about hydration and victory. She sat down.

Micah leaned over and whispered, "Zero. I counted zero, and I was ready for anything."

"Owned the world," Alexandre whispered back, "like a penguin."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
story:
Lillian kept one eye on the warm-ups and one eye on the folded paper in her pocket. Ms. Byrne had posted the league standings in the gym hallway that morning: Kennedy's team first, Lillian's team second. That was all it said. No numbers, just names in order, and second place felt like it was glaring at her.

"Stop looking at it," said Kianna, snapping a pass against the wall. "You've read it nine times. Ten, now."

"It intimidates me," Lillian admitted. "They're first. Like they're untouchable." But even as she said it, something snagged in her mind. She thought about the swim finals they'd watched in science class during free period, when the silver medalist touched the wall a hundredth of a second after the winner. Same podium, same order, and then another race where the silver medalist lost by a whole minute. Both times, the list had just said first, second, third. The ranking showed who beat whom. It never showed by how much. Maybe Kennedy's team was way ahead. Maybe they were ahead by almost nothing. The standings alone couldn't tell her. She needed to be systematic about it, so she dug through her bag for the crumpled sheet of game scores she'd been keeping all season.

At halftime a text buzzed on the phone the coach held up for the bench. It was from Kennedy: "Check the points column. You're gonna lose your mind."

Lillian added the columns twice on the back of her water bottle label, breath held, because a hundredth of a second and a whole minute are not the same thing at all. The totals came out the same both times. One game. They were behind by exactly one game, out of a whole season, with tonight's rematch still on the clock.

Fourth quarter, forty seconds left, down by two. Kianna drove the lane, got swallowed by three defenders, and flicked the ball out to Lillian alone at the arc. The rim rattled. The gym held its breath.

"Next year," Kennedy whispered at the handshake line, and bumped fists with her anyway.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Shoveling heavy snow is hard work for the heart, so doctors advise taking breaks and lifting small loads rather than big shovelfuls.
story:
William woke to a white blur outside the window and a radio voice saying school was postponed until tomorrow. A whole surprise snow day, and the drifts in the backyard came up past the picnic table. He was still grinning when he noticed something that made him stop: Mr. Taylor next door, out in his driveway with a shovel, scooping huge armfuls of wet snow and flinging them aside, then pausing with one hand pressed against his coat.

Macie knocked on the fence a minute later, mittens already on. "Did you see him?" she whispered. "He's been at it since seven. My grandma says shoveling heavy snow is hard work for the heart, so doctors advise taking breaks and lifting small loads instead of big shovelfuls. He's doing exactly the wrong thing." William looked at the ominous grey sky stacking more clouds over the rooftops, then at Mr. Taylor bending for another giant scoop. The snow was the antagonist here, and the old man was losing.

"Come on," William said, and they crunched across both backyards with his spare shovel. "Mr. Taylor! Want some help?" Mr. Taylor straightened up slowly, cheeks red. "It'll take you kids all day," he puffed.

"Then we'll take turns," Macie said. "One row each, then a rest. William, you go first, but fill the shovel only halfway. Small loads."

William tried it. A half-full shovel felt almost too easy, like cheating, but he began to wonder about it. Four rows in, he wasn't winded at all, while Mr. Taylor's big scoops had left him gasping in half that time. Was it because the small loads added up the same but spread the work out? He decided to test it. He counted his scoops down one row: eleven small ones instead of maybe six huge ones, and no burning in his arms, no pounding in his chest. On his rest breaks he watched Macie work, and a pattern showed up clear as footprints. Whoever lifted small and stopped between rows finished faster, because they never had to stop in the middle to catch their breath.

They cleared the driveway in under an hour, then the walk, then a path to the mailbox just because it felt good. Mr. Taylor sat on his porch step with hot cocoa from his kitchen, and he didn't look grey anymore, only pleased. He held up his mug toward the yard.

"So the snow thinks it won today," he said. "Let's see what it thinks about tomorrow."
